LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & FIRST OBJECTS · AGES 3–4 MONTHS

Yellow circle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Yesterday was red; today the circle comes back in yellow. This lesson uses that single change to smuggle in the biggest idea of the set: what the word "colour" is actually about.

What is this?

Yellow is the second colour card: the same round shape your baby met in red, now in a bright, sunny shade. The shape staying constant is the whole trick — the only thing that changed is the colour, so colour is what gets noticed.

What does it mean?

Babies spot change before they spot categories. When everything about an image stays put except one feature, the growing brain flags that feature as "what this thing is about". Two circles, one red and one yellow, quietly define colour for your baby.

What does the child need to know?

Show yellow on its own first, then bring the red card alongside. Name them in turn — red... yellow — with a pause between, so each word lands on its own colour. Do not expect your baby to match or prefer anything; preference is a bonus, not a goal.

Why this matters

A baby who has seen "same shape, different colour" twice has the beginnings of comparison: how are these alike, how are they not? That question will one day sort animals, letters, numbers and people. It starts with two paper circles.

What it teaches

Colour discrimination, same-and-different noticing at the earliest level, visual comparison across two cards, and turn-taking in narration.

Words to learn

yellowredcirclesamedifferentsunny

Say this to your child

“"Yellow! A big yellow circle, bright as the morning. And here comes our old friend — red. Red circle, yellow circle. The same shape in two different dresses. Look at them both, side by side."”

Step by step

  1. Settle your baby and show the yellow circle alone at close range, naming it twice: "Yellow. A big yellow circle."
  2. Give it a good long look — at least ten seconds of nothing but the card and your quiet.
  3. Bring the red circle into view beside it, matched for height and distance, and name them in turns: "Red... and yellow."
  4. Let your baby’s eyes travel between them as long as they like; a slow sway of one card restarts a stalled gaze.
  5. Finish with whichever colour held the longer look — say that colour’s name once more as the last word, then tidy away.

Look closer at the picture

The artwork is one large yellow circle, the red card’s exact twin in a new shade — say that much. Then watch the real event: do the eyes move between the two colours, or settle on one? Whichever happens is your baby’s honest answer today.

Ask your child

Watch the travel: does the gaze cross from yellow to red and back, or camp on one? Does the same colour win two days running? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if you like the new one best because it is new."

What your child can say or do

Side-to-side looking between the cards, a longer gaze on one colour, an excited leg-kick when the second card appears, or a drowsy drift that ends things early — every version counts, and the drift is a full stop, not a fail.

Out in the real world

Yellow lives in kitchens and walks: a banana on the counter, a rubber duck on the bath edge, dandelions in the grass. One tap, one "yellow" each time — the second meeting of the word does more than the first ever could.

Try it together

Lap swap: show yellow, then red, then yellow again across your lap, letting your body be the card stand. Your baby’s head turns become the game — you are strengthening neck control and colour memory in the same five minutes.

Understanding check

Parent self-check: did the two colours actually meet this session, and did you pause between their names? The pause is what keeps the words from blurring into one — say them like two separate gifts.

Parent tips

Keep the shape talk minimal — the circles are alike on purpose, and that is enough. If your baby ignores yellow entirely, do not chase it; tomorrow’s blue is a fresh chance. Never audition colours against each other like a contest.

Staying safe

Two cards in play means two cards in your hands or folded away — nothing rests on the baby’s chest or beside them on the mat. Swats happen: accept them against the held card, and check for dented edges before the next session.

This lesson pairs with the Yellow circle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & First Objects (Infant 1).
